precepts.text: Blessed is the man that doth meditate good things in wisdom, and that reasoneth of holy things by his understanding. When we do not study, we have nothing in our spirits to combat Satan; we are defenseless. Even Christ, when he was tempted, used the word of God: is it not written? When you meditate good things, you can reason in the scriptures: wait, the scripture says this; I cannot do that. When you go before the magistrates, think not what ye shall say; but you have to have something in your spirit for the Lord to work with. If you have no scriptures about lust in your head, where are you going to pull from? Give the Holy Spirit something to work with. When Joseph was tempted, he referred straight back to the law: I would be sinning against God. That was what came to his mind first, because his mind was always on the scriptures.
precepts.point: Wherefore, my dearly beloved, flee from idolatry. Why is idolatry the word here? Because you idolize these temptations. That appetite, the lust within you, becomes an idol to you: you idolize that demon inside of you and you feed it, and it is never enough.
precepts.why:
“There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able”. The Lord still gives you enough strength not to be overtaken, and always a way out. But it is up to you. Sometimes we are weak in the faith and weak in the spirit: you don't read your four chapters a day, your conversation is not about the scriptures, you are not around the brothers, and Satan gets a hold of you.

When we do not study, we have nothing in our spirits to combat Satan; we are defenseless. Even Christ, when he was tempted, used the word of God: as it is written. We have to be the same way. Sirach: “Blessed is the man that doth meditate good things in wisdom, and that reasoneth of holy things by his understanding.”

When you meditate on good things, you can reason in the scriptures in the moment of temptation: wait, the scripture says this; I can't do that. “He that considereth her ways in his heart” is always asking, what does the scripture say about this? That is how you combat the lust, the demon: you have to have something in your spirit.

When you go before the magistrates you are told not to think about what you will say, but you still have to have something in your spirit for the Lord to work with. If you have no scriptures about lust in your head, where are you going to pull from? Give the Holy Spirit something to work with. When Joseph, our forefather in Egypt, was tempted, he went straight back to the law: I would be sinning against God. That came to his mind first because his mind was always on the scriptures. Temptation always comes with an exit; addiction forms when we stop taking the exit.

precepts.text: All flesh waxeth old as a garment, for the covenant from the beginning is, Thou shalt die the death; as the green leaves, one generation cometh to an end and another is born.
precepts.point: Not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think soberly. If God has revealed himself to you, humble yourself before the King of kings.
precepts.why:
“All flesh waxeth old as a garment: for the covenant from the beginning is, Thou shalt die the death.” That is what we just read in David: seventy, maybe eighty years. That is the covenant God pronounced from the beginning: thou shalt die the death.

“As of the green leaves on a thick tree, some fall, and some grow; so is the generation of flesh and blood, one cometh to an end, and another is born.” That is why we have kids. You watch them grow up, and you say, man, I'm getting old. You know the covenant God pronounced upon all flesh, and you are about to cross it too.

“Every work rotteth and consumeth away, and the worker thereof shall go withal.” That is the covenant: thou shalt die the death, thus saith the Lord. Everything a man builds goes with him. So there is no room to think of yourself more highly than you ought; think soberly, knowing the covenant is coming for you like every other leaf on the tree.

precepts.text: The envious man hath a wicked eye; that is the eye Saul eyed David with, and the iniquity of the wicked dried up his soul.
precepts.point: And Saul eyed David from that day and forward. What was behind that eye? Envy. The envious man is not satisfied with his own portion; Saul had his thousands and still had the kingdom, but his eye was on David's portion, and iniquity dried up his soul from that point forward.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

precepts.why:
“And Saul eyed David from that day and forward.” What was behind that eye? Envy. “The envious man hath a wicked eye; he turneth away his face, and despiseth men.” That is the eye Saul eyed David with.

“A covetous man’s eye is not satisfied with his portion.” Saul had his thousands and he still had the kingdom, but his eye was on David's portion: “what can he have more but the kingdom?”

Then: “and the iniquity of the wicked drieth up his soul.” From that point forward, that iniquity dried up Saul's soul.

precepts.text: A covetous man's eye is never satisfied with his portion.
precepts.point: As the fining pot for silver and the furnace for gold, so is a man to his praise. Though you bray a fool in a mortar with a pestle, his foolishness will not depart from him.
precepts.why:
“Hell and destruction are never full; so the eyes of man are never satisfied.” Eyes that are never satisfied go into covetousness.

Ecclesiasticus says it plainly: “A covetous man’s eye is not satisfied with his portion; and the iniquity of the wicked drieth up his soul.” The covetous man's eye is never satisfied with his portion, and that iniquity dries up his soul. Like hell and destruction, it never gets full.

We are meant to be satisfied with our own portion. The eye that is never satisfied is the covetous eye, and it is the wicked whose soul it dries up.
